EXTRACTS from the ANNUAL REPORT 
of the BOARD OF DIRECTORS 


As Presented at the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association held 
in the Westmount Building, May 20th, 1915. 


ia BE 


of us perhaps the most remarkable in our experience. 

The great struggle now raging on the continent of Europe 
and elsewhere increasingly absorbs our interest and attention, 
and both directly and indirectly touches the life and work of 
our Association. 


a Na year through which we have passed has been for all 


The feeling of uncertainty as to the future which prevailed in 
July and August last year led us to adopt a policy of the most 
rigid economy. At the same time we felt that as far as pos- 
sible we must keep our organization well in hand so that we 
might respond quickly to new opportunities which were sure 
to arise. 


The immediate effect of the war upon our work is best 
realized when we remember that the large volume of immi- 
gration which formerly came to us from Great Britain and the 
continent and which had much to do with Canada’s prosperity 
as well as enlarging the activities of our own Association has 
now practically ceased, while on the other hand thousands of 
our best young men have enlisted and gone to the war. Fur- 
thermore, many of those who remained have had their salaries 
or wages reduced or have been obliged to return to the places 
from whence they came and there wait a revival of that pro- 
sperity which originally attracted them to the city. 


Notwithstanding these adverse conditions, the reports of 
the various branches as presented at their Annual Meetings 
have given every evidence of good work and in some cases show 
improvements over last year. We think the difficulties with 


3 


which we have had to contend have been good for us and we 
feel confident that the work is in a good condition and ready 
to take full advantage of the opportunities for enlargement 
which will come in due time. 


We present the following summary of our membership as 
on April 30th, 1915.

We have the names of 267 members of the Association who 
have enlisted for the war, many of whom are now at the front. 
These men come from our branches as follows :— 


Railroad Branch...........----------------+---- 11 
Westmount Branch.........-..-----------+-------- 28 
North Branch... a.-------------s0-sseeesseeeeoeseens 44 
Central, Men's Dept....- LAS sf

Metropolitan Board Staff_........----------- I 

Titel eset sek ee re ave ews e is 5 LOOP, 


Let us hold them in the highest honor and remember with 
gratitude their unselfish and loyal service for our King and 
Country. 


Special Work for Soldiers —Following the outbreak of war 
we at once considered what might be done for our soldiers in 
training. Our Canadian National Council acted with great 
promptness and efficiency, and the work done at Valcartier 
merits our highest praise. Owing to shortness of staff, Mr. 
A. C. Johnston, our physical director at Point St. Charles, was 
the only man we could spare to assist at Valcartier. Simul- 
taneously with the opening of the Peel Street barracks for the 


4 


23rd and 24th Battalions, a special Military Committee was 
appointed with Mr. R. C. Holden as Chairman. This Commit- 
tee has rendered excellent service during the intervening 
months. 


A marvelous opportunity has been presented to the Asso- 
ciation for helpful ministry amongst more than twenty million 
men who are now in arms engaged in this gigantic struggle. 
It is encouraging to note how fully the Associations throughout 
the world have pressed the advantage. We hope that some 
day the story will be fully written. 


Work Amongst Foreign Speaking Young Men.—Last year the 
Association made a careful investigation as to the conditions 
under which the more than 100,000 foreigners in our City live 
and, as a result, invited Mr. F. W. Bagnall, a graduate of 
Acadia University, Wolfville, N.S., to undertake special work 
for us amongst these people. Mr. Bagnall joined our staff on 
July 24th, but, shortly after the war broke out, enlisted with 
the Grenadier Guards, and is now serving at the front with 
the 14th Battalion. 


In June last, Messrs. G. E. Williams and W. E. Cushing were 
appointed Advisory Members of the Board of the Italian 
Y.M.C,A. 


The Chinese Association has sought closer affiliation with 
our Board, and practical methods of accomplishing this are 
being worked out. 


Point St. Charles Branch.—Early last summer, negotiations 
were opened with the Grand Trunk Railway Company for the 
taking over of the Point St. Charles Building by the Company 
for railroad use. Owing to unfavorable financial conditions, 
the matter is in suspense. In August, the restaurant con- 
ducted by the Branch was closed. In October, the Company 
rented rooms for the use of the apprentice classes. 


East End Branch.—Mr. W. A. MacLaren, a former member 
of our Staff, entered upon his duties as Secretary of this Branch 
on September 1st. On May ist, the Branch moved to new 
quarters across the street at a reduced rental. The growing 
interest of the members is seen in the fact that they have 
assumed the rental of the Branch for the coming year in addi- 
tion to the local expenses. 


Southwark Railroad Branch—The opportunity at this point 
promised well a year ago but traffic did not revive in the Fall, 


5 


and after trying the matter out thoroughly, the Company 
decided to move the Terminal back to Turcot. We were obliged, 
therefore, to close this Branch on January 15th last. 


Mention should be made of the patriotic action of Messrs. 
Evans. Lorimer, Cooper and Virgo of the Central staff, who 
enlisted last October and are now in England with their re- 
spective commands. 


The Association has been specially indebted during the 
year to Mr. Henry Birks for a gift of $1,000.00 towards the. 
Library at the Central Branch. 


The Association has also been advised of a legacy of $250.00 
by the will of the late Mr. William Wainwright, a life-long 
friend of the Association. 


J. W, KNOX, President, 
C, K. CALHOUN, General Secretary.
